weeks.trajectory_note: This is the first tracked week, so there is no prior baseline for week-over-week movement; all ten situations are 'new' by definition and all changes/arrows are set to zero/steady accordingly. The starkest pattern in this baseline is the split between conflicts with the highest casualty tolls (Sudan, the Sahel insurgency, Myanmar, DRC) and their comparatively minimal presence in global/English-language media, versus conflicts with strong strategic or political salience (Taiwan, Gaza, Yemen's Red Sea dimension) that draw attention somewhat independent of current casualty counts. Russia-Ukraine and Haiti are the closest to proportionate coverage given their severity. None of this should be read as a claim that heavily-covered conflicts don't deserve their coverage — the point is that severity and newsworthiness are measured on different bases, and the biggest blind spots (the Sahel and Sudan in particular) are worth watching for whether coverage improves or the gap widens as these wars continue.

weeks.trajectory_note: The largest development this week is procedural rather than a single battlefield swing: this tracker added the US-Israel war on Iran (ongoing since Feb 28, 2026) to the registry for the first time, having omitted it in prior passes. Within the reporting window the war expanded geographically (first strike reaching Egypt, Iranian retaliation against Kuwait) even as US-Iran talks are reported to resume in early August — a pattern of parallel escalation and negotiation rather than clear movement in either direction. Separately, the Gaza-Israel conflict saw its first concrete disarmament roadmap (Jul 31), a genuine diplomatic step but one Israel has not yet accepted and which has not altered on-the-ground violence, so it is scored as a modest, claim-level de-escalation rather than a resolved shift. Sudan, the Sahel insurgency, Myanmar and DRC remain the most severe and most structurally underreported situations in the tracked set, a pattern that has been stable since week 29 and looks set to persist as long as the Iran war and Gaza dominate the global news cycle. Note for continuity: week 30 (Jul 20-26) was not produced, so this entry's arrows/changes are computed against week 29 (Jul 13-19) as the most recent available baseline rather than the immediately preceding calendar week; this gap should be flagged in any longer-run trend analysis.

weeks.trajectory_note: Two of the week's largest tracked conflicts moved in opposite directions on real, implemented evidence rather than announcements: the DRC/M23 conflict saw its first concrete prisoner exchange under the Doha process (a genuine, if modest, de-escalation signal), while the Israel-Iran-US war saw substantive technical progress toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz (route coordinates agreed, though full reopening remains contingent on unresolved US concessions) alongside a new regional defense pact (Saudi Arabia-Turkiye-Pakistan) signed against that war's backdrop. Gaza moved the opposite way: last week's disarmament announcement did not translate into reduced violence — strikes intensified, July was confirmed the deadliest month of the year, and West Bank settler violence hit its worst level since October 2023 — so this week's score reverses part of last week's claim-level de-escalation, consistent with protocol.md's evidence hierarchy (enforced outcomes outweigh announcements). Sudan, the Sahel insurgency, Myanmar and DRC remain the most severe and most structurally underreported situations in the tracked set, a pattern stable since week 29; Taiwan and the Israel-Iran-US war remain the most overreported relative to rank, now joined by a modestly widening gap as Iran-war coverage stayed at saturation levels even as the war's own evidence moved toward de-escalation. The overall pattern — severe, low-visibility conflicts in Africa and Asia persisting alongside intense coverage of conflicts with direct US/Western or global-economic stakes — looks structural rather than shifting.

weeks.trajectory_note: The week's most significant single development is diplomatic rather than kinetic: Netanyahu's public rejection (Aug 10) of the US-brokered 15-point Gaza plan removes the clearest path to resolution that had existed since the Jul 31 disarmament announcement, even as Israeli strike tempo itself fell sharply this week (two deaths on Aug 13 versus dozens in prior weeks) — a reminder that diplomatic and kinetic trajectories can move in opposite directions in the same conflict within the same week. The Israel-Iran-US war continued its slower, more consistent de-escalation, with Iran and Oman narrowing toward a Hormuz reopening deal, though the DRC/M23 process shows the limits of diplomacy without enforcement: talks toward a comprehensive peace agreement remain nominally on track for an Aug 18 signing, but ground clashes in Kalehe continued through this window with no new confidence-building measure comparable to last week's prisoner exchange. Myanmar produced the week's strongest new evidentiary development: a UN-mandated investigative mechanism, not a media outlet, documented a deliberate and escalating pattern of aerial attacks on civilians using new low-cost aircraft, which both raises its severity score and modestly narrowed its historically wide coverage gap. Sudan, the Sahel insurgency, DRC and Myanmar remain the most severe and most structurally underreported situations in the tracked set, a pattern that has now held steady since week 29; the Israel-Iran-US war, Gaza and Taiwan remain the most overreported relative to rank, driven by direct Western involvement, sustained political salience and, for Taiwan, the novelty of its largest-ever military exercises rather than any current casualties. This structural blind-spot pattern shows no sign of shifting.
